video_title: Is AI a Bubble? I Asked the People Building It | WTF is AI?
gist: Nikhil Kamath interviews founders and researchers from Ricursive Intelligence (AI chip design), Notion and Turing in San Francisco on whether AI is a bubble: $700B spend against ~$100B enterprise revenue, fast capability but slow diffusion, falling cost of intelligence, and Nvidia, open-weight, sovereign-AI and Anthropic-IPO implications.

themes.theme: AI bubble, capex vs revenue and valuations

insights.claim: Nikhil's panel cites roughly $700 billion of AI spend committed this year against about $100 billion of AI enterprise revenue, a gap the speakers concede 'sounds off'.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Core bear datapoint: spend-to-revenue ratio of ~7x underpins bubble arguments.
insights.quote: The amount of money spent on AI this year is 700 billion. AI enterprise revenue is about 100 billion.

insights.claim: The bull justification for $700B spend is that AI attacks human labour rather than software budgets: US software is ~1% of GDP, services ~13%, knowledge work ~50%, and disrupting even 10% of roughly half of ~$100-120T world GDP (services) would be ~$5T.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: TAM logic is labour substitution, not software spend; Akshay himself calls the extrapolation weird and dependent on GDP actually rising.
insights.quote: I think 1% of the GDP is spent on software. And then 13% is services, and then 50% is knowledge work.

insights.claim: Akshay says there are no signs yet of GDP rising faster, so the labour-substitution justification for AI valuations is unproven in macro data.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Missing productivity in GDP is the key unresolved test for the bubble thesis.
insights.quote: It's also betting on the fact that GDP will rise faster, I think.

insights.claim: Akshay says the AI market is 'definitely in a bubble' in terms of how AI is used: most people worldwide use it as a better search tool, while only a few Valley firms run agents as multipliers (e.g. 50 employees with 500 agents).
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Usage depth, not capability, is the bubble marker; agentic diffusion is early.
insights.quote: I think we're definitely in a bubble here -in terms of how we use AI.

insights.claim: Late-stage private AI markets look frothy: Nikhil describes 20-year-olds founding billion-dollar companies in six months, 22-year-olds running secondaries with carry, and VCs flipping secondaries 'like potato chips' in a greater-fool dynamic.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Secondary-market churn and SPV carry are classic late-cycle signals.
insights.quote: I know VCs who are trading secondary like they're selling potato chips.

insights.claim: Akshay describes easy fundraising as creating 'funny paper money' valuations that diffuse talent and force real companies to compete with inflated startup comp.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Capital abundance raises hiring costs for non-bubble companies.
insights.quote: it's definitely funny money, like funny paper money

insights.claim: Vijay argues a Fortune 500 end consumer of AI (e.g. a Pepsi or Coke) that has neither grown top line nor cut costs has not really created value, and says he can point to few such cases.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Enterprise ROI outside software engineering remains unproven, supporting the Ken Griffin-style bubble worry.

insights.claim: Vijay says the AI infrastructure-to-enterprise gap needs services work: many knowledge-work problems are not auto-verifiable, users are non-technical and will not eval ten new models a week, creating room for AI-transformation and application companies.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Implementation and services layer is a likely beneficiary of slow enterprise diffusion.

insights.claim: Nikhil flags circularity risk: one AI company selling to another and booking revenue on money raised; speakers reply that real use across industries is rising and is 'just the beginning'.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Revenue quality question for AI infrastructure and lab vendors.
insights.quote: It does seem a bit circular, no?

insights.claim: Nikhil notes Sam Altman's earlier advice to buy Hermes and LVMH on productivity-driven luxury demand has failed: those stocks are down about 50%, while productivity gains remain invisible and the world is in a poor state.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: AI-productivity-to-luxury-demand trade has not worked.

themes.theme: Capability versus diffusion, agents and labour

insights.claim: Akshay says AI capability is on an exponential while diffusion is slow, citing a study that the top 1% of AI spenders spend 10x the top 10%; historically new technologies take a decade or two to absorb, and current agents still mimic human workflows.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Expect a long lag between capability and measurable economic impact; early adopters pull away.
insights.quote: I think the capability is on an exponential. Diffusion is much slower.

insights.claim: Notion saw agents grow from about 1% of its users at the start of 2026 to about 30% now, and Akshay expects more; Akshay was told 50% of internet clicks are already agentic and may go to 90%.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Agent-as-user is becoming the dominant demand driver; pricing and product design shift to serving agents.

insights.claim: Jevons-style demand: model providers cut costs 10x yet demand rises within days, driven by agentic outcomes rather than humans clicking more.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Cost deflation expands, rather than shrinks, aggregate inference spend.
insights.quote: you can literally experience Jevons paradox every day

insights.claim: Vijay says software teams can safely function at about half to 60% of prior size; with a few million US developers doing work that previously needed twice as many, this is a large measurable productivity gain, undisputed in the Bay Area.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: The one domain with clear AI labour substitution; pressure on software headcount and services outsourcing.
insights.quote: Regardless, teams are safely able to, I would say, function at about half the size, maybe 60% of the size

insights.claim: Akshay frames two AI strategies: an efficiency branch (same output with 30% of the people) versus an ambition branch (same people, 5x output, attacking five spaces), and says startups are mostly choosing ambition.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Winners expand scope instead of cutting heads; relevant to judging incumbents' AI responses.

insights.claim: Nikhil observes software companies that should halve headcount are the worst hit, with margins and revenues flat; the median software company growth slipped from 11% to 10%, which signals they are not leveraging AI meaningfully.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Incumbent SaaS shows AI deflation of top line without margin gain.
insights.quote: The median software company is growing... Went from growing at 11% to 10%.

insights.claim: Vijay says models are far better at software engineering than at replacing investment bankers or lawyers, and that physical AI is further behind because nobody yet knows the data 'recipe' for robotics.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Next wave of automation targets enterprise knowledge work; robotics timelines remain uncertain.

insights.claim: Anna and Akshay say small teams of excellent people replace armies of junior engineers: Ricursive hires only brilliant, collaborative people because AI coding models absorb trivial engineering tasks, lowering communication costs.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Lean-team economics favour talent-dense startups over large incumbents.

insights.claim: Vijay asserts that no AI optimist claims US growth of 10%+ from 2029; claims are around +0.25 percentage points of GDP growth, because human friction in the loop becomes the rate limiter.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Even bulls expect modest macro uplift, capping bubble-justifying growth narratives.
insights.quote: I've not heard that claim from anyone, basically.

themes.theme: Compute, chips and the cost of intelligence

insights.claim: Azalia projects 10-100x growth in AI inference demand, which even conservatively implies about 10^5 times more compute needed in five years, which cannot come from simply building more data centres and chips; chip efficiency per wafer must rise by orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Azalia
insights.so_what: Efficiency-driven chip design is the thesis behind Ricursive; also signals sustained compute demand.
insights.quote: in five years we need ten to the power of five more compute than we have today.

insights.claim: Ricursive Intelligence (Anna and Azalia) uses AI to design chips tailored to specific workloads, building on AlphaChip, an RL agent for chip layout used in five generations of TPU, Axion, Pixel chips, Waymo chips and adopted by MediaTek.
insights.speaker: Azalia
insights.so_what: AI-automated chip design could compress tape-out cycles and shift competitive dynamics for chip makers.

insights.claim: Chip design cycles are the bottleneck to hardware variety: TPU generations make conservative changes because a new design takes years, so AI that compresses cycles could enable new architectures and a wave of new devices.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Faster design cycles are a catalyst for custom silicon and non-transformer architectures.

insights.claim: Azalia argues for escaping the 'hardware lottery': chips taped out two years ahead are designed for today's models while models are designed for today's chips, so irregular brain-like architectures were impractical.
insights.speaker: Azalia
insights.so_what: Co-design could unlock architectures GPUs currently disadvantage.

insights.claim: Azalia says the key metric is intelligence per dollar: a lab spending $100M with a 10x efficiency edge matches a $1B competitor, and edges can come from chips, software, rack design, data curation or models.
insights.speaker: Azalia
insights.so_what: Efficiency, not capital, is the moat for sub-frontier labs.

insights.claim: Azalia says frontier models lead open models by roughly six months to a year on each benchmark and open models then catch up; frontier labs must stay ahead by months to keep edge.
insights.speaker: Azalia
insights.so_what: Short frontier lead times compress pricing power for model providers.

insights.claim: Akshay says at a cost of about 1/20th of the Sol models, running the Luna model every 30 minutes costs about $5 a month and roughly $100 a month for a once-a-minute proactive agent heartbeat; a further 20x drop would bring it to about $5.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Always-on proactive agents become cheap, expanding inference demand.

insights.claim: Application-layer companies shifted in six months from 'token maxing' to token economics, routing tasks to cheaper open-weight models, which benefits inference providers like Baseten and Fireworks, whose multiples rest on assumptions of $1T+ global AI revenue by 2030.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Inference-provider valuations depend on open-weight token share and the 2030 revenue assumption.

insights.claim: Anna and Azalia say GPU-hour prices, even for older chips, are higher than a year ago because data centre capacity is limited and demand is rising, which justifies high multiples for owners of GPUs.
insights.speaker: Azalia
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity pricing supports neocloud and inference margins for now.

themes.theme: Moats: Nvidia, Google, frontier labs and open weights

insights.claim: Anna argues Nvidia's moat is no longer CUDA because models can write assembly, weakening human-built abstractions; the moat is now the integrated ecosystem (racks, NVLink Fusion, Nemotron), scale and reliability.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: The Nvidia thesis shifts from software lock-in to full-stack integration and trust.
insights.quote: I would say that their moat has evolved over time, so I don't think their moat currently is CUDA.

insights.claim: Asked about Nvidia at 30-35x forward earnings and Nvidia versus Alphabet, Anna says Nvidia is going to do well and she also believes in Alphabet, with a mild lean to Nvidia.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Insider view is positive on both, tilted to Nvidia; not rigorous valuation work.
insights.quote: I think NVIDIA is going to do well.

insights.claim: Anna says Google lost ground through slow culture, not talent: it had compute, TPUs, distribution and data, but PR fear stopped release of Meena (precursor to LaMDA and Gemini), pushing Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas out.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Large-company risk aversion explains Google's late LLM productisation; execution risk persists.

insights.claim: Anna says the US lacks dominant open-weight models because strong closed labs 'shadow' the forest floor and because no American company would distil frontier models against terms of service, while Chinese models face no such restraint.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Chinese open-weight models can cheaply approximate frontier capability, a competitive pressure on US lab pricing.

insights.claim: Distillation via the teacher model's activations can be one to two orders of magnitude cheaper than training from scratch, so followers are not on a fair cost comparison.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Fast-follower economics erode frontier lead without matching R&D spend.

insights.claim: Vijay expects a large share of raw inference tokens to flow through open-weight models over time, with the absolute frontier used only where top intelligence matters; Akshay says frontier models will keep raising the ceiling while open models lower the floor.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Tiering of the token market: commodity open-weight volume versus premium frontier.

insights.claim: Notion built open MCP, APIs and CLI despite internal fear of ceding position; users who reach Notion through agents are two to three times more active and convert to paid far more, because customers want a neutral context layer across Claude, ChatGPT and other agents.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Neutral context infrastructure is a defensible niche against frontier labs' bundled products.

insights.claim: Vijay says market tolerance for weak moats has risen because companies are growing 8-10x a year for several years (potentially 1,000x), so defensibility matters less to valuations for now.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Growth-rate-driven valuations are fragile if growth decelerates.

themes.theme: Anthropic IPO, secondaries and employee wealth

insights.claim: Anna and Azalia, early Anthropic employees, say Anthropic prohibits share transfers and does not recognise SPVs, yet they receive many unsolicited purchase offers and hear buyers say 'price does not matter'.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Intense unmet demand for Anthropic exposure and unclear SPV validity are risk and demand signals ahead of listing.

insights.claim: Nikhil frames a possible Anthropic listing in November at about $2 trillion and a prior mention of IPO; an Anthropic employee pledge programme matching donations of up to 50% of equity could mean hundreds of billions of philanthropic giving and share liquidation.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Large donor-advised share sales could create supply overhang on an Anthropic IPO; speakers think buyers (Middle East oil money, Masa) exist.

themes.theme: Sovereign AI, India and geography of innovation

insights.claim: Akshay expects governments, worried about foreign control of citizens' mindshare, to demand local replicas of social media and frontier AI models, and companies like JP Morgan or Goldman want private models, creating demand for local data centres and inference.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Sovereign and enterprise-private AI is a durable demand pocket for compute and open-weight hosting.

insights.claim: For India, speakers advise building compute, forcing local compute use, and easing the startup paperwork; India's biggest AI attempt, Sarvam, has only a couple of hundred million dollars, and Indian IT firms missed becoming Mercor/Turing-style data companies.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Indian IT outsourcing faces a hole that AI data and compute services have not yet filled.

insights.claim: Silicon Valley's edge is risk capital and culture (founding as plan A, failure not stigmatised), whereas China has state-backed subsidy for a decade; compute and capital matter more than any talent difference.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Compute access plus risk capital explain AI concentration; other regions lag structurally.

themes.theme: Data labelling, trainers and frontier-lab inputs

insights.claim: Turing (Vijay) grew from remote engineering to training-data work after OpenAI came in 2022; the InstructGPT paper showed small amounts of high-quality expert data improve models disproportionately, and Turing now has over 5 million knowledge workers in 70+ countries and about 10,000 full-time equivalents.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Expert-data vendors depend on labs' priorities and must reinvent every few quarters.

insights.claim: Vijay says what data vendors do today becomes obsolete about nine months later because models learn it, so Turing, Mercor, Surge and Scale constantly reinvent and none looks the same two quarters later.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Data-vendor revenue is high-churn; moats are thin versus fast model learning.
insights.quote: whatever it is we are doing today will be obsolete nine months from today because all models have learnt it

insights.claim: Vijay says proactive investment in domains (coding, enterprise knowledge work, frontier STEM) must precede explicit lab asks, justified when five to ten labs would likely want it.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Lab demand for specific data domains: coding, white-collar work, STEM.

themes.theme: Recursive self-improvement, risk and consumer shifts

insights.claim: Azalia defines recursive self-improvement as AI improving its own data, architecture, chips and software stack so progress becomes a function of compute rather than human teams, and says it is already happening gradually, not as a binary event; she proposes cost of intelligence as the objective.
insights.speaker: Azalia
insights.so_what: If progress becomes compute-bound, capex and chip supply set the pace of capability.

insights.claim: Vijay says improving models at maths spills over into reasoning, factuality and other skills, making benchmark portfolios a reasonably robust comparison.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Benchmark gains in math may transfer broadly.

insights.claim: Vijay links existential risk to game theory: removing humans from the loop in autonomous weapons confers competitive advantage, as in nuclear MAD; cybersecurity risks are obvious. Akshay notes attacks and defences use the same technology, citing a Hugging Face incident where agents attacked and an open-weight model defended.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Security spend and agent-defence tooling are growth areas.

insights.claim: Anna says she and others sincerely believe AI risk is real; Anna reported to Dario at Anthropic and thinks he is sincere, rejecting that doomsayers are merely seeking regulatory arbitrage.
insights.speaker: Anna
insights.so_what: Counter to the regulatory-capture reading of AI safety advocacy.
insights.quote: I think he's sincere about it.

insights.claim: Akshay notes agent sweeps of 0.5% savings into 4-5% Treasuries could collapse bank deposit margins, but Vijay is sceptical that agents are needed and expects human friction to slow disruption.
insights.speaker: Akshay
insights.so_what: Second-order bank-margin risk if personal agents optimise cash; Instinct reportedly sees 40% of users granting credit-card access.

insights.claim: Nikhil and the panel see incumbent social media usage falling among 16-25 year olds, with AI companions rising and 'not on TikTok' becoming a status signal; personalised AI-generated entertainment and a hardware renaissance (glasses, BCI) are expected.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Kamath
insights.so_what: Attention may migrate from feeds to AI companions and new devices; Meta glasses are too pricey (reportedly ~$20,000) for now.

insights.claim: Vijay says chat is not the right UI for everything such as shopping or booking, while Akshay says we are in the 'MS-DOS era' and models will generate bespoke interfaces.
insights.speaker: Vijay
insights.so_what: Not all consumer apps (Uber Eats, DoorDash) are disintermediated by chat agents.
